front.title: The DataReel gxStream Database Block Protocol and Object Replication over TCP Port 2073

abstract.t: This document describes gxStream, the database block protocol of the DataReel C++ library, and the services carried on it: the DataReel database object server with its channel multiplex, remote access to database objects and vector searches, and gxObjRepl object replication between two independent object databases. gxStream runs over TLS with certificates on both sides on TCP port 2073, which is registered with IANA under the service name "gxs-data-port". The port was registered before a protocol description was required; this document provides that description, as implemented in DataReel 7.5. It is published for information and does not specify an Internet standard.

note.name: Note
note.t: This is an Independent Submission. The protocol is defined by its reference implementation, the DataReel library, which is free software under the GNU Lesser General Public License version 3 or later (https://datareel.com). Where this document and the DataReel 7.5 source differ, the difference is listed in .

section.name: Introduction
section.t: DataReel is a cross-platform C++ library with an embedded object database and TLS communication classes. Since 1999 it has had a block protocol, gxStream, that carries database blocks between programs: the same block header the database writes before every object in its files is sent on the network, followed by the block's bytes. TCP and UDP port 2073 were registered with IANA for this protocol as "gxs-data-port", "DataReel Database Socket".

DataReel 7 (2026) rewrote the protocol on TLS: no block is ever sent or accepted in cleartext, servers require client certificates by default, and every length received is checked before it is used. DataReel 7.3.1 added the database object server, which carries several services over one listener and a multiplex of independent channels. DataReel 7.4 added vector searches to the object service, a canonical block header on every platform, and gxObjRepl, which replicates objects (never file pages) from a primary node to a copy. DataReel 7.5 added the incremental rejoin to gxObjRepl and a Python package that uses the same protocol.
This document specifies:

ul.li: the transport and TLS requirements ();
the gxStream block and its control codes () and the basic block exchanges ();
the database object server's service selection ();
the channel multiplex (), the object service and vector searches ();
the gxObjRepl replication protocol ().

section.t: DataReel 6.x, the legacy release line, can also carry gxStream blocks over plain TCP and over UDP. These legacy transports are described in for completeness; they have no authentication or encryption and are NOT RECOMMENDED.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document describes an existing protocol. The requirement words state what an implementation needs to do to interoperate with DataReel 7.5 (and 7.4) and to keep its security properties.

section.name: Terminology

dl.dd: A 32-byte block header followed by zero or more body bytes.
The TLS client (the side that opens the TCP connection) and the TLS server.
A record stored in a DataReel database file, identified by its file address on one node or, in replication, by a 64-bit object id shared by both nodes.
One independent stream of messages inside a multiplex session.
The replication node that takes writes, and the node that receives them.
A replication generation number, raised by each takeover.

section.t: Integer types are written u8, u16, u32 and u64 (unsigned, 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes), i64 (signed, 8 bytes, two's complement) and f32 (IEEE 754 binary32). Unless a section says otherwise, every integer and float is sent in little endian byte order.

section.name: TCP
section.t: gxStream runs over TCP . Servers listen on port 2073 unless configured otherwise, and clients connect to port 2073 unless given another port. A server MAY listen on IPv6 and IPv4 at once. Implementations SHOULD disable the Nagle algorithm on replication connections, since each frame is answered by a small acknowledgment.

section.name: TLS
section.t: Every gxStream connection MUST be protected with TLS. The TLS handshake starts immediately after the TCP connection is established; there is no cleartext phase and no STARTTLS command.

ul.li: Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 and SHOULD support TLS 1.3 . They MUST NOT negotiate SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1, and SHOULD follow in the choice of cipher suites.
Neither side may send or accept a block before the handshake has completed. An implementation MUST NOT send blocks on, or accept blocks from, a connection whose handshake failed or was not run.

A client MUST send the server name indication extension when it connects by host name, and MUST verify the server's certificate chain and the server's identity (DNS name, or IP address for a numeric host). Partial-label wildcards MUST NOT be accepted. A failed check closes the connection before any block is sent.

A gxStream server SHOULD require a client certificate. Such a server MUST verify the client's chain against a configured set of client certification authorities only (not a general trust store) and MUST accept only clients named in a configured allow list, by the SHA-256 fingerprint of the certificate or by its subject common name (exact, case sensitive match). A server that accepts clients without certificates MUST be configured to do so explicitly.
No application-layer protocol negotiation (ALPN) identifier is used. The service is selected by the first block ().

section.t: A failed handshake, failed certificate check or failed allow list check closes the TCP connection.

section.name: Timeouts
section.t: Every handshake, read and write SHOULD be bounded by a timeout. DataReel 7.5 uses 10 seconds for the handshake and 120 seconds for each block on the database object server, 30 seconds for the replication handshake and hello, and a configurable idle timeout (default 120 seconds) for replication frames.

section.name: Block Header
section.t: Every block begins with a 32-byte header of four 64-bit little endian words:

dl.dd: 0x000000000000FEFE. A receiver MUST treat any other value as a loss of synchronization and close the connection.

The number of body bytes that follow the header. The high 32 bits MUST be zero; a sender MUST NOT send a block longer than 2147483647 bytes. A receiver MUST compare the length with its maximum block size before it allocates memory for the body, and MUST close the connection if it is larger.

Byte 0 (the least significant byte) is the data status. Senders set it to 0x56 ("V", a block received from a remote device); receivers MUST ignore it. Byte 1 is the control code (). Bytes 2 to 7 MUST be zero.
A signed 64-bit value carried by a result block (); zero in every other block.

section.t: The high four bytes of the Check Word and of the Status word are always zero. A receiver that finds a non-zero byte there has met a peer that sends the obsolete header with 32-bit words (a 24-byte or 16-byte header sent by DataReel builds older than 7.4 beta 5 on 64-bit Windows, or by 32-bit builds). It MUST close the connection and SHOULD report that cause; it MUST NOT try to read the block.
The block header is the one DataReel writes before each block in its database files; on the network the Result word carries what the file uses as a free list pointer.

section.name: Control Codes
section.t: The control code is one ASCII character:

tr.td: The body is a new object to add.
The body names an object to change; an "S" block with the new contents follows.
The body names an object to delete.
Header only. Asks the server to shut down.
Header only. The sender is done with the connection.
The body is a request; the reply is a block.
The body is data: a reply, a multiplex frame or a replication frame.
Header only. Asks the server to restart.
Header only. An acknowledgment; the Result word carries the result.

section.t: Other code values are defined in the DataReel headers for database file use or for earlier designs and are not sent by the services in this document. A server MUST close a session that sends a code its service does not expect. "K" and "T" give a client control over the server process: a server MUST NOT act on them unless the client is authorized to administer the server; the DataReel 7.5 database object server does not act on them and closes the session.

section.name: Maximum Block Size
section.t: Each receiver has a maximum block size. DataReel 7.5 uses 67108864 bytes (64 MiB) by default and 17825792 bytes (17 MiB) on the database object server. A sender SHOULD NOT send a block larger than the peer is known to accept: multiplex senders split messages into frames of at most 1 MiB (), and replication limits objects to 32 MiB and commits to 60 MiB.

section.name: Basic Block Exchanges
section.t: The original gxStream exchanges use the control codes directly. The object service accepts them from DataReel 6.x style ("legacy") clients ().

dl.dd: The client sends an "R" block whose body is the request; the server answers with one "S" block whose body is the reply (possibly empty).
The client sends an "A" block whose body is the object; the server answers with a result block.
The client sends a "C" block whose body names the object, then an "S" block with the new contents.
The client sends a "D" block whose body names the object.
A "W" header with Length 0 and the result (for example a file address, 0 for none) in the Result word.
A "W" header with Length 0 and Result 0.
An "L" header. The receiver closes the session.

section.name: The Database Object Server
section.t: The DataReel database object server carries several services on one listener. After the TLS handshake and the client certificate checks, the server reads the session's first block and gives the session to the first service that claims it:

ol.li: An "S" block whose body is a multiplex HELLO frame (): the multiplex, with the object service on its channels.
An "A" or "R" block: the legacy object service, if the server is configured with a legacy database.

section.t: A first block that no service claims closes the session. The first byte of a multiplex body is 0x4D ("M"); services that use "S" blocks for other messages MUST NOT start their first message with that byte.

To resist connections that never complete TLS, a server SHOULD run each handshake apart from its accept loop with a short timeout and a limit on concurrent handshakes (DataReel 7.5: 10 seconds, 16 handshakes), and SHOULD limit the number of authenticated sessions (DataReel 7.5: 4 by default). Only sessions that passed the certificate checks count against the session limit.

section.name: Legacy Object Sessions
section.t: On a server configured with a legacy database:

ul.li: An "A" block adds its body as a new object. The reply is a result block with the new object's file address, or 0 if the add failed (for example because the database is read-only).
An "R" block whose body is an 8-byte object address is answered with an "S" block holding that object, or an empty "S" block if there is none.
An "L" block ends the session. Any other block also ends it.

section.name: The Channel Multiplex
section.t: The multiplex carries numbered channels over one connection. Each channel has its own order, flow control and errors, so one slow or failed channel does not hold up the others.

section.name: Frames
section.t: Each multiplex frame is one "S" block. Its body is an 18-byte frame header followed by the payload:

dl.dd: The frame kind, 1 to 9 ().
The channel number. Channel 0 is the connection itself (HELLO, and CLOSE of the whole connection).
For DATA frames, a per-channel counter starting at 1 and increasing by 1 for each DATA frame the sender sends on the channel. Control frames carry 0.
Bit 0 (LAST) marks the last DATA frame of a message. Other bits MUST be zero.

section.t: In payloads, "str" is a u32 length followed by that many bytes, and "bytes" is a u64 length followed by that many bytes. Every length MUST be checked against the remaining payload; a payload that is too short is malformed.

tr.td: str service, str name, str mode, u64 credit

section.t: A block that is not an "S" block, or whose body is not a frame (shorter than 18 bytes, a wrong mark, an unknown kind), ends the connection. An "L" block ends the connection.

section.name: Session and Channels

ol.li: The client sends HELLO on channel 0. The server answers with its own HELLO. A side that receives a HELLO with another magic string or version MUST end the connection. A client MUST send HELLO before any OPEN.

The client opens a channel with OPEN, choosing an unused non-zero channel number. The payload names the service ("object" for ), the object to open (a database name) and the mode ("read" or "write"), and gives the opener's receive credit ().

The accepting side answers OPENED (with its own credit and optional service data) or REFUSED (with a reason). It MUST refuse an OPEN on channel 0, on a channel that is open, or with a malformed payload.
Either side sends DATA on an open channel. A message is a run of DATA frames ending with one that has the LAST flag.
Either side closes a channel with CLOSE, or with ERROR and a reason. A CLOSE on channel 0 ends the connection. DATA that arrives for a closed channel is discarded.

section.t: Frames of one channel are delivered in the order they were sent; TLS over TCP provides that order. ACK frames are passed to the channel's consumer in order with its DATA frames; a service uses them to report that the data up to a DATA sequence number is durable at a log sequence number (lsn) of its own.

section.name: Flow Control
section.t: Flow control is per channel and counts DATA payload bytes only; control frames are not counted.

ul.li: Each side's credit for a channel starts at the value the other side gave in OPEN or OPENED: the size of its receive queue for that channel (DataReel 7.5: 16 MiB).
A sender MUST NOT send a DATA frame larger than its remaining credit, and subtracts each DATA payload from the credit as it sends it.
As the receiver's consumer takes data, the receiver returns the room with CREDIT frames. DataReel 7.5 sends CREDIT when a quarter of the queue has been consumed, or when the queue becomes empty.
A receiver MUST count the DATA bytes it has received on each channel and, if they exceed the credit it has granted in total, MUST close the channel with ERROR ("over credit").

Senders SHOULD NOT send DATA payloads larger than 1 MiB, and SHOULD share the connection between channels fairly. DataReel 7.5 sends control frames first, then DATA frames by deficit round robin with a quantum of 256 KiB.

section.name: The Object Service
section.t: The object service gives remote access to the objects of the databases a server is configured with. A client opens a multiplex channel with service "object", the database name and mode "read" or "write". The server MUST refuse the open for a database it does not serve, for any other mode, and for mode "write" on a database that is read-only or is a replicated copy.

section.name: Requests and Replies
section.t: Each request is one message: a u8 operation followed by its arguments. Each reply is one message: a u8 status (0 success, 1 error) followed by the result on success, or by a str (u32 length and bytes) with the error on failure. An empty request message closes the channel with an error.

ul.li: Addresses are the object's file address in the server's database; address 0 is never an object.
ADD, CHANGE and DELETE are refused on a channel opened "read". On a writable database each one is one durable transaction. CHANGE MUST carry exactly the object's existing length.
Reads of a replicated copy MUST NOT observe a partly applied replication commit.
A request whose arguments do not exactly fill the message is malformed and answered with an error.

section.name: Vector Searches
section.t: A database configured with a vector index answers VECTOR_SEARCH and VECTOR_INFO on any channel, read only. The VECTOR_SEARCH arguments are, in order: u32 version (1); u32 k (1 to 1000); u32 ef (0 for the server default of 64, at most 4096); u32 dim (MUST equal the index's dimension); u32 flags (bit 0: apply the day range; bit 1: strict, a missing index file is an error; other bits MUST be zero); u32 tag_mask (bits 0 to 3; other bits MUST be zero); u32 lo[4]; u32 hi[4] (when bit i of tag_mask is set, tag i must be within lo[i]..hi[i]); u32 day_lo; u32 day_hi; and f32 query[dim]. The arguments MUST be exactly that long and every query value MUST be finite.

The VECTOR_SEARCH result is: u32 version (1); u32 count; u32 files skipped by their day range; u32 files missing; count entries of { i64 id, f32 distance, u32 tags[4], u32 file }, sorted by distance, then file, then id; u32 names; and names entries of { u32 file, str path } for the files the results name, with paths relative to the index manifest's folder.
The VECTOR_INFO result is: u32 version (1), u32 dim, u32 element type, u32 metric, u32 files, u64 nodes, u64 deleted, str spec.
A server SHOULD limit concurrent searches; DataReel 7.5 runs at most 4 at once and answers a search that waits more than 5 seconds for a slot with the error "busy".

section.name: Object Replication (gxObjRepl)
section.t: gxObjRepl replicates the object databases of a primary node to a copy node. Only objects travel; each node keeps its own file addresses, free space and indexes. Objects are identified by 64-bit ids shared by both nodes. Replication is asynchronous.

section.name: Connection
section.t: The primary is the TLS client and the copy is the TLS server. The copy MUST require a client certificate from the configured certification authority with the configured subject common name; the primary MUST verify the copy's certificate and identity ().

Each replication frame is the body of one "S" block. The copy answers each frame with exactly one "S" block. The primary sends the next frame only after it has the answer. In this section a "str" is a u16 length followed by that many bytes.

The copy handles one primary connection at a time. It closes the connection, without an answer, when a frame breaks the rules below; it SHOULD record the reason where an administrator will see it (DataReel writes an alarm file).

section.name: Hello and Reply
section.t: The first frame on each connection is the primary's hello:
section.artwork: hello = u32 magic ; 0x3550524F ("ORP5" in byte order) u64 epoch ; the primary's epoch str link-map ; link fields, "DB:OFFSET:TARGET_DB,..." str name ; the primary's node name u8 role ; 1 (primary) u64 last-seq ; the primary's last commit u64 digest ; the running digest at last-seq ; since DataReel 7.5 (optional, see below): u32 rj-magic ; 0x31304A52 ("RJ01" in byte order) u64 base-seq ; the seq at which this primary took over u64 base-digest ; the running digest at base-seq str fingerprint ; the schema fingerprint
section.t: The copy answers:
section.artwork: reply = u8 ok ; 1 accepted, 0 refused u64 applied-seq ; the last commit the copy applied u64 epoch ; the copy's epoch u8 in-full-send ; 1 if a full send is under way str name ; the copy's node name u8 role ; 2 (copy) u64 digest ; the running digest at applied-seq str why ; the reason when ok = 0 ; since DataReel 7.5 (optional, see below): u32 rj-magic ; 0x31304A52 u8 incremental ; 1 if the copy takes an incremental rejoin str fingerprint ; the copy's schema fingerprint
section.t: The copy MUST refuse (ok = 0, then close) a hello that is malformed or has another magic number; a hello received while the copy is itself a primary; a role other than 1; a name other than the configured peer name, if one is configured; an epoch lower than the copy's; a last-seq lower than the copy's applied-seq when no full send is under way; a malformed link map; or, when the copy has its own link map configured, a link map that differs from it or link fields that overlap the copy's index fields.

The primary MUST stop (and SHOULD raise an alarm) when the reply has ok = 0, a role other than 2, or a name other than its configured copy name. Unless the copy is in a full send or has applied nothing, the primary MUST also check the copy's history: applied-seq MUST NOT exceed the primary's last commit, and the copy's digest MUST equal the primary's digest at applied-seq. A primary that no longer knows its digest at that sequence MUST refuse the copy; an administrator then has the copy rejoin.

The fields after the rj-magic are optional in both directions. A receiver that finds fewer than 4 bytes after the fields above, or another magic number, MUST treat the peer as one that does not have them (a DataReel 7.4 node), and MUST ignore bytes after the fields it knows. A primary sends base-seq 0 when it has no recorded takeover. The schema fingerprint is the text "index=SPEC;links=MAP;schema=TEXT": the node's index specification and link map, each in a canonical order, and the application's record layout version (free text of at most 200 characters, no ";"). Outside an incremental rejoin a fingerprint that differs is not a reason to refuse; an implementation SHOULD log it.

Having accepted the copy, the primary sends F_EPOCH (). The copy MUST refuse every other frame kind on the connection until it has received F_EPOCH. The copy saves the epoch durably on F_EPOCH, never at the hello, so that a primary that then refuses the copy cannot fence out the real one.

section.name: Frames
section.t: Each frame starts with a u8 kind:

tr.td: u64 seq, u64 epoch, u32 ops, ops
u64 base seq, u64 digest, u64 count, u64 hash
u32 entries, entries of {u64 seq, u64 digest}
u64 base seq, u64 up-to seq
u8 ok, u32 entries, entries of {str database, u64 id}
u64 up-to seq, u64 digest, u64 count, u64 hash

section.t: An answer is an "S" block whose body is at least 8 bytes; its first 8 bytes are the u64 shown. The answer to F_RJ_SET is the exception: its body is the u8, u32 and entries shown. A frame of an unknown kind is refused. Frames 7 to 9 are used only by DataReel 7.5 and later, in an incremental rejoin ().

section.name: F_COMMIT
section.t: Each op is: u8 op (1 ADD, 2 UPDATE, 3 REMOVE, 4 PURGE), str database, u64 object id; ADD and UPDATE then carry u32 capacity (the record size the primary allocated), u8 moved (1 if the object moved to a new block on the primary), u32 length and that many bytes of object data. In the object data, every link field named by the link map carries the target's object id instead of a file address (0 for no link).
A database name consists of letters, digits, "_" and "-" only. The copy MUST:

ul.li: refuse a commit whose epoch is lower than the copy's epoch, or that arrives during a full send;
answer a commit whose seq is not greater than its applied-seq with its applied-seq, without applying it again (a resend);
refuse a commit whose seq is not applied-seq + 1 (a gap);

apply all ops of the commit in one durable transaction, translating each link from an id to its own file address (creating a placeholder for a target it does not have yet), raise its epoch to the commit's epoch if that is higher, and answer with seq only after the transaction is durable. A commit that cannot be applied is rolled back and not answered.

section.t: REMOVE leaves a tombstone that keeps the object's id and address, so links to it still resolve. PURGE frees a tombstone.

section.name: Full Send
section.t: When the copy is in a full send, or the primary no longer has the commits that follow the copy's applied-seq, the primary sends a full copy of its databases as of its last commit (the base):

ol.li: F_SNAP_BEGIN with the base and the epoch. The copy records that a full send is under way, sets its current data aside (it is not deleted until the full send ends) and starts empty. A copy MUST refuse F_SNAP_BEGIN with an epoch lower than its own.

F_SNAP_BATCH frames. Each record is: str database, u64 id, u32 version, u32 flags (bit 0: tombstone), u32 reason, u64 seen seq, u32 capacity, u32 length, and that many bytes (links as ids). The copy MUST refuse a batch outside a full send, and records whose length exceeds 32 MiB or whose capacity is too small for the data.
F_SNAP_DLOG frames with the primary's digest log up to the base (at most 65536 entries a frame), so that the copy can later prove its history.

F_SNAP_END with the base, the running digest at the base, the number of batch records and digest log entries sent, and a hash chained over them. The copy MUST refuse an F_SNAP_END whose base differs from F_SNAP_BEGIN, or whose count and hash differ from what it received; the full send then stays open and the primary sends it again. Otherwise the copy translates all links, sets its applied-seq to the base and its digest to the given digest, ends the full send and answers with the base.

section.t: The commits made on the primary after the base then follow as F_COMMIT frames.

section.name: Incremental Rejoin
section.t: After a takeover the former primary may hold commits the new primary never received. Since DataReel 7.5 such a node can rejoin as a copy without a full send. Each node records, at every takeover, the epoch it took over at with the sequence number and running digest it had then (its epoch base), and, for each commit it makes as a primary, the databases and ids that commit changed (its change list). A former primary that is to rejoin records which of its commits were never acknowledged, with what they changed, and waits for an incremental rejoin.

At the hello such a copy MUST answer incremental = 1 only when the primary sent the optional fields, base-seq is not 0, the copy's own digest at base-seq equals base-digest, and the two schema fingerprints are equal. When the fingerprints differ, the copy MUST refuse the primary (ok = 0): its data cannot be patched, and an administrator rebuilds it with a full send into an empty node. In the other cases it answers incremental = 0 and takes a full send ().
When the copy answered incremental = 1, the primary MAY send, instead of a full send:

ol.li: F_RJ_SET with its base-seq and its last commit (up-to). The copy MUST refuse it unless it answered incremental = 1 on this connection, up-to is not below the base and it has a digest at the base. It drops its digest log entries after the base, records that an incremental rejoin to up-to is under way, and answers with ok = 1 and the (database, id) of every object its own commits after the base changed. When that list does not fit one frame it answers ok = 0 with no entries, and the primary sends a full send instead.

F_RJ_BATCH frames. Each record is either u8 1 followed by a full-send record (: the object as it is now on the primary, or its tombstone), or u8 2, str database, u64 id: the primary has no such object, and the copy removes it. The primary sends a record for each object of the copy's list and of its own change list after the base. Records are checked as in a full send; each batch is applied in one durable transaction before it is answered.
F_SNAP_DLOG frames with the primary's digest log after the base, up to up-to.

F_RJ_END with up-to, the running digest at up-to, the number of batch records and digest log entries sent, and a hash chained over them (). The copy MUST refuse an F_RJ_END whose up-to differs from F_RJ_SET's, or whose count and hash differ from what it received; the rejoin then stays open and the primary sends it again on a later connection. Otherwise the copy translates the links of the objects the batches wrote, sets its applied-seq to up-to and its digest to the given digest, ends the rejoin and answers with up-to.

section.t: The commits made on the primary after up-to then follow as F_COMMIT frames. A node that stops in the middle of an incremental rejoin keeps waiting for one and finishes on the next connection.

An implementation SHOULD bound the work of an incremental rejoin: DataReel sends one only when the objects to send are at most a configured share of the primary's objects (50 percent by default), and a full send otherwise.

section.name: Digests
section.t: The running digest is the 64-bit FNV-1a hash (offset basis 14695981039346656037, prime 1099511628211) chained over the bytes of every F_COMMIT frame body in sequence order: it starts at the offset basis, and each commit continues the hash from the previous value over the whole frame body, from its kind byte to its last op. The primary computes it when it records a commit; the copy when it applies one. Each node keeps a log of (seq, digest) pairs for at least the last 1000000 commits.

The full send hash is the same FNV-1a function chained, from the offset basis, over the bytes of each F_SNAP_BATCH record and of each 16-byte F_SNAP_DLOG entry, in the order sent. The incremental rejoin hash is computed the same way over each F_RJ_BATCH record (from its leading u8) and each F_SNAP_DLOG entry.
These digests detect divergent histories and lost, repeated or altered frames caused by faults. They are not cryptographic and do not authenticate the stream ().

section.name: Epochs, Takeover and Rejoin
section.t: A node starts at epoch 1. A takeover makes a copy the primary at its epoch plus one. Object ids that a primary issues carry its epoch in bits 40 and above, so a new primary never issues an id that an older primary may have issued in commits the new primary never received. Every copy that has saved the new epoch refuses an older primary. A former primary rejoins as a copy that waits for a full send, which replaces its databases, or, since DataReel 7.5, for an incremental rejoin ().

section.name: Port
section.t: Replication is a gxStream object stream and uses TCP port 2073. A copy listens on port 2073, and a primary connects to port 2073, unless configured with another port; a host that runs a copy and another gxStream service on the same address gives one of them another port. DataReel 7.4.1 makes 2073 the default of both settings; DataReel 7.4 had no default.

section.name: Legacy Transports (DataReel 6.x)
section.t: DataReel 6.x is the legacy release line (bug fixes and security updates only). Its gxStream and gxDatagram classes predate the TLS requirement of . Since DataReel 6.4 they send the same canonical block header as DataReel 7.4 () and check received lengths before allocating memory. Both transports below are described so that implementations and network operators can recognize them; neither meets the requirements of this document.

section.name: gxStream over Plain TCP
section.t: A DataReel 6.x gxStream client uses TLS only when the program enables it. A DataReel 6.4 gxStream server refuses to accept clients unless it either uses TLS with client certificates and an allow list (as in ) or the program explicitly opts out; a server that opts out without a server certificate exchanges blocks over plain TCP. Blocks on such a connection have no confidentiality, integrity or authentication. New deployments MUST NOT use plain TCP, and DataReel 7 does not support it.

section.name: gxDatagram over UDP
section.t: The DataReel 6.x gxDatagram class sends blocks over UDP : each block is one datagram holding the 32-byte block header, followed by one datagram holding the body (so a body is at most 65507 bytes). The control codes and exchanges of apply. There is no retransmission, ordering, encryption or authentication: any host that can reach the port can send blocks, and a lost or reordered datagram leaves the two sides out of step. Receivers check the header form and the length against a maximum before reading the body.

This is the use for which UDP port 2073 was registered. gxDatagram is not part of DataReel 7, and implementations of this document do not use UDP. New deployments MUST NOT use gxDatagram on networks where any host is untrusted.

ul.li: Block level: a wrong check word, an oversize length, non-zero reserved header bytes, or a read or write failure ends the connection.
Multiplex: a malformed frame ends the connection; a refused open, an over-credit channel, an ERROR or a CLOSE ends that channel only.
Object service: a request error is a reply with status 1 and a message; the channel stays open.

Replication: a refused hello is answered with ok = 0 and a reason; any other violation closes the connection without an answer. The primary connects again on its next attempt and the hello checks start over.

section.name: Confidentiality and Integrity
section.t: All traffic is protected by TLS (), and implementations refuse to send or accept blocks before the handshake completes, so there is no cleartext mode to downgrade to. The block header, the multiplex and the replication frames add no cryptographic protection of their own. Implementations should require TLS 1.3 where both peers support it. With TLS libraries that offer a hybrid key exchange such as X25519MLKEM768 (ML-KEM ), recorded traffic is protected against a future quantum computer; certificates remain RSA or ECDSA.

section.name: Authentication and Authorization
section.t: Servers authenticate clients by certificate (mutual TLS) and an allow list. Server certificates are checked against the server's name. Authorization is by service: a certificate in the allow list may use every database the server serves, in every mode the server's configuration allows for that database. A client allowed "write" access can change or delete any object of that database. Deployments that need finer authorization should run separate servers or databases per client group.

A server MUST accept a client-supplied object address only if it is the start of a live object of that database: the block header in front of it must be valid and not deleted, the block must lie inside the file, and the address must be a block boundary rather than a place inside another object, whose bytes a client may have written to look like a block header. DataReel 7.4 checked only the header's check word, so a client with write access could damage the database it may change and a client with read access could read deleted blocks; DataReel 7.4.1 makes the full check for writable databases ().

section.name: Replication
section.t: A peer whose certificate the copy accepts is trusted with the stream. Such a peer can raise the copy's epoch, which fences out the legitimate primary, or replace the copy's data with a full send. The epoch, sequence and digest checks protect against operational mistakes (a stale primary, two primaries, a diverged history); they do not protect against a compromised key. Replication keys should be dedicated to replication, kept readable only by their owner (DataReel refuses a key file that group or others can read), and the copy's allow list should name only the primary.

section.name: Resource Exhaustion
section.t: Every length received is checked against the remaining data and against a maximum before memory is allocated. Servers limit concurrent handshakes, handshake time, sessions and concurrent vector searches, and the multiplex bounds each channel's queue with credit. An attacker who can reach the port can still occupy handshake slots for the handshake timeout, and a replication copy, which serves one connection at a time, can be delayed by a connection that stalls its handshake. The number of channels in one multiplex session is not limited in DataReel 7.5. Access to port 2073 should be limited by firewall to the hosts that need it, and servers used only locally should listen on the loopback address.

section.name: Server Control Codes
section.t: The "K" (kill) and "T" (restart) control codes let a client stop or restart a server process. They must not be honored for clients that are not authorized administrators; DataReel 7.5 servers do not honor them.

section.name: Stored Data
section.t: The legacy DataReel 6.x transports () carry blocks in cleartext and, over UDP, without any peer authentication. Operators should block them at the network edge and replace them with TLS connections.
DataReel database files are not encrypted by the library; data is protected on the wire, not at rest. Block check words and optional CRC-32 checksums in the files detect accidental damage only.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: IANA has assigned port 2073 for TCP and UDP in the "Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry" :
section.artwork: Service Name: gxs-data-port Port Number: 2073 Transport: tcp, udp Description: DataReel Database Socket
section.t: This document asks IANA to update the Reference of the TCP assignment to this document, keeping the service name, port number, assignee and contact.

The UDP assignment is used only by the legacy DataReel 6.x gxDatagram transport (). This document asks IANA to update the Reference of the UDP assignment to this document as well, and otherwise to keep it unchanged while DataReel 6.x is maintained.
This document creates no new registry. The control codes, multiplex frame kinds, object service operations and replication frame kinds are maintained by the DataReel project with its source code.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: This section follows . The reference implementation is the DataReel C++ library , release 7.5, on Linux (OpenSSL) and Windows (Schannel or OpenSSL), and the datareel Python package built from it. Release 7.4.1 implements everything except the optional hello fields and , and interoperates with 7.5. The DataReel 6.4 legacy release sends the same block header and interoperates with 7.4 and 7.5 over TLS. Files: include/gxheader.h, include/gxstream.h, src/gxstream.cpp, include/gxstls.h, src/gxstls.cpp, src/gxdbserver.cpp, src/gxdbmux.cpp, src/gxdbobject.cpp, src/gxobjrepl.cpp.

The DataReel 6.4 legacy release (6.4.1 and the 6.4.2 branch) implements the block header and the basic exchanges in its own gxStream class (include/gxstream.h, src/gxstream.cpp), with TLS, client certificates and an allow list as in , and also the legacy transports of (src/gxdatagm.cpp for UDP). Its optional dr7features library links the DataReel 7.4 code for the object service client (vector searches) and for gxObjRepl replication, so a 6.4 program and a 7.4 program replicate to each other with the protocol of . The utils/objrepl/xver tests of DataReel 7.4 check 6.4 and 7.4 peers against each other, and utils/objrepl/test_objrepl_rejoin.sh checks 7.4.1 and 7.5 replication nodes against each other.
Known differences between DataReel 7.5 and this document, to be resolved in a later 7.5.x release:

ul.li: The high 32 bits of the Length word are not checked on builds where the in-memory length field is 32 bits wide (Windows, and builds without native integer types); the length is truncated instead of refused. Such a block then fails the next header check. The multiplex reader also does not check the reserved high bytes of the Check Word and Status words.

The object service of DataReel 7.4 checked a client-supplied object address only by the check word of the block header in front of it. DataReel 7.4.1 requires a valid, not deleted block inside the file, and for a writable database one of its live objects. A read-only database, opened for each request, does not check that the address is a block boundary: an address behind a block header copied into an object's bytes can still be read there (bytes of the same file only).
The multiplex server does not require HELLO before OPEN, and does not limit the number of channels in a session.
DataReel 7.4 had no default replication port; 7.4.1 uses 2073 ().
Multiplex and object service integers are sent in the host byte order. Every platform DataReel 7.5 supports is little endian, so this matches the little endian order specified here.
